newsitem.title: BULGARIA: New Bulgaria president may face fresh clashes.
newsitem.headline: New Bulgaria president may face fresh clashes.

text.p: Bulgaria's new president Petar Stoyanov took office in a colourful religious and military ceremony on Wednesday, inheriting economic crisis, political deadlock and the threat of fresh violence.

Student protesters symbolically buried the ex-communist ruling Socialists at the mausoleum of Bulgarian communist hero Georgi Dimitrov, as the party approved potentially explosive counter-protests against daily opposition rallies.

"Local party structures should assess the necessity of mass action supporting giving a second mandate to the Left," Valery Radev, regional party leader from the mining town of Bobov Dol, near Sofia, said after a Socialist leadership meeting.
Counter-rallies by supporters of neighbouring Serbia's Socialist President Slobodan Milosevic in Belgrade on December 24 led to clashes between demonstrators and riot police.
Stoyanov, elected on the opposition ticket in November, took over command of the army from outgoing president Zhelyu Zhelev at a military parade outside the presidency.
He then received the blessing of the Orthodox church in the first religious ceremony for a new head of state since Boris III became king in October 1918.
Bulgaria's Orthodox church has not been spared the divisions dogging the rest of society, but Stoyanov's religious ceremony included the two rival patriarchs.
Stoyanov received the blessing of Patriarch Pimen, who split from the synod with his followers after 1989, accusing the official Patriarch Maxim of being a stooge of the former communist regime.
Maxim, who said a separate mass in Sofia's gold-domed cathedral, greeted the president when he arrived for the blessing ceremony at the site of daily opposition rallies.
The president, who has cancelled the usual champagne reception as inappropriate at a time when hundreds of thousands of Bulgarians are hungry, laid a wreath at the memorial to the nation's war dead.
He then walked back to the presidency, surrounded by enthusiastic crowds who cheered him and booed outgoing Socialist prime minister Zhan Videnov.
Some 5,000 students accompanied by hundreds of teachers and lecturers carried a coffin draped with a red communist flag through the streets in their daily protest.

Weeping women prostrated themselves as a band played funeral marches. One banner bore tables showing the lev's decline against the dollar to make a professor's monthly salary worth the equivalent of $35.
On Thursday Stoyanov, a lawyer who specialises in divorce cases, is to hold more talks with government and opposition on finding a way out of Bulgaria's political deadlock.
He backed opposition calls for early elections at his swearing-in ceremony last Sunday in the parliament, which was besieged and ransacked by demonstrators on January 10.

Under its post-communist constitution, Bulgaria is a parliamentary republic whose president is a mainly ceremonial figure. He represents the country in its foreign relations, appoints ambassadors, judges and some other officials, and can veto laws once and send them back to parliament.
The president also has the task of asking the prime minister nominated by the largest parliamentary group to form a government, which Zhelev has refused to do in the present explosive atmosphere.

The Socialists have offered elections in December, a year ahead of schedule, but in the meantime they want to form a new cabinet following Videnov's resignation last December 21. The opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) wants elections in March.

Government corruption and the Socialists' resistance to reform have left Bulgaria lagging behind other eastern European states. Annual inflation is running at more than 300 percent and a flight into dollars pushed the lev to a new all-time low on Wednesday of 800 to the dollar from about 70 a year ago.
